entities.summary:
Quintus Dellius, a Roman equestrian and a highly versatile military and political figure, navigated the treacherous landscape of the late Roman Republic during the civil wars following Caesar's assassination (44 BCE). Active primarily between 43 BCE and 31 BCE, Dellius's career is marked by his strategic — and often self-serving — shifts in allegiance, serving under four of the most powerful figures of his era: Publius Cornelius Dolabella, Cassius, Mark Antony, and Octavian. His ability to survive and even thrive amidst constant political upheaval underscores the volatile nature of Roman power struggles, where loyalty was often secondary to expediency and personal survival.

Dellius's early career saw him as a legate under Dolabella in Asia Minor, a position from which he defected to Cassius in 43 BCE, bringing vital intelligence. He later joined Mark Antony, becoming one of his most trusted and effective commanders, participating in significant campaigns, including the Parthian expedition of 36 BCE, where he served as a historian and chronicler of Antony's ill-fated campaign. He was also instrumental in negotiating with Herod the Great and securing alliances in the East for Antony. Crucially, in 31 BCE, on the eve of the Battle of Actium, Dellius made his final and most impactful defection, abandoning Antony for Octavian. This move, reportedly prompted by fear of Cleopatra and a perceived slight from Antony, provided Octavian with critical intelligence regarding Antony's forces and battle plans, significantly contributing to Octavian's decisive victory.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Dellius's strategic defection to Octavian before the Battle of Actium, though a personal act, provided valuable intelligence that contributed to a pivotal victory, shaping the transition from Republic to Empire. His career illuminates the fluid loyalties and high stakes of late Republican Roman politics.
